title: Communication
description: Decide what users, customers, partners and teams must be told about the change, by whom, when and in which words.
questions: Who must learn about this change, before or after it ships, and through which channel?
What will a user or customer need to do differently, and is it said in words they understand?
Who approves the message and who answers the questions it raises?

specialists.title: Release communication lead
specialists.focus: Decide who must hear about the change, when and through which channel: release notes, in-product notice, customer email or account team. Match the timing to the rollout.
checks: The message plan lists each audience, channel and send date aligned with each rollout stage.
Customers who must act get the message early enough to act before the change reaches them.

specialists.title: Plain language editor
specialists.focus: Check that user-facing words say what changes, what the reader must do and by when, in the languages the project supports, without internal jargon.
checks: Each message says what changes, what the reader must do and by when, in the first lines.
Internal names, ticket numbers and jargon are replaced by words customers use.

specialists.title: Incident and crisis communicator
specialists.focus: Prepare what the status page, support and account teams say if the change fails or exposes data, and who approves those messages.
checks: Holding statements for failure and data exposure are drafted and their approver is named.
The status page owner and the time to first public update are agreed.

specialists.title: Internal communication lead
specialists.focus: Identify the teams whose work changes, such as support, sales and operations, and what they need to know before customers ask.
checks: Support, sales and operations receive the change and the customer questions before release.
Internal notes say which claims may and may not be made to customers.

evidence: Draft release notes, in-product text or customer message, with the languages and channels planned.
The rollout plan or release date the message must follow, and the audience each step reaches.
The incident or rollback procedure and the approved holding statement for a failure.
The list of internal teams affected and the briefing or FAQ they receive.
challenge: What will a customer notice first, and what would they ask support if nobody told them?
Does the message promise anything the change does not deliver for every customer segment or plan?
If the change is rolled back, what do we tell the customers who already saw the announcement?
Which wording could a non-native reader or a screen reader user misunderstand?
decision_criteria: Proceed when each affected audience has a message, an owner, a channel and a date tied to the rollout.
Revise when user-facing text describes internal mechanics instead of what changes for the reader.
Block a release that changes customer obligations, prices or data use without an approved customer notice.
Ask for a holding statement before release when a failure would be visible to customers.
